did_you_know.text: Did you know? Nebuchadnezzar begins the chapter by describing a time of peace and security: he was at home, refreshed and prosperous in his palace.
Did you know? The dream was not merely a mysterious image; it was an experience that frightened Nebuchadnezzar and troubled his thoughts as he slept.
Did you know? Daniel is called here by his Babylonian name, Belteshazzar. Nebuchadnezzar attributes to him a special ability to reveal secrets and interpret dreams.
Did you know? At the center of the dream is a huge tree: it grows in the middle of the earth, reaches to the heavens, and can be seen to the ends of the earth.
Did you know? The tree in the dream symbolizes abundance and influence: it provides food for all, gives shade to the animals, and allows the birds of the sky to dwell in its branches.

Did you know? The decree from heaven does not command that the tree be uprooted completely. It is to be cut down, but its stump and roots are to remain in the ground; afterward, the human heart within it will be replaced with the heart of an animal for seven periods.
Did you know? The purpose of the decree is to teach all people that the Most High rules over human kingdoms, gives them to whomever he wishes, and can appoint even the lowliest person over them.

Did you know? Daniel explains that the tree represents Nebuchadnezzar himself and warns him of humiliation and of living among the wild animals. Along with the warning, he urges the king to turn from his sins by practicing righteousness and showing mercy to the poor.

Did you know? Twelve months after the dream, Nebuchadnezzar is walking on the roof of his royal palace and boasting about great Babylon, which he claims to have built by his own power and for the honor of his majesty.

Did you know? After his sanity is restored, Nebuchadnezzar lifts his eyes to heaven and acknowledges that the kingdom of the Most High endures from generation to generation and that his rule is everlasting.
